title: write the 8 bytes immediately before an object: where an allocator keeps its header
object: a, 24 bytes; the write covers a-8 .. a-1
neighbour: glibc keeps the chunk size there; a bump arena keeps nothing; a free list may keep its own header
control: writes the object's own first 8 bytes
note: The ground-truth counterpart of capstone's memsys5 in-band free-list demonstrator: an allocator that stores bookkeeping next to or inside user blocks turns a small write into corruption of itself. Which is why `none` (no tool) is an interesting column here: it records whether the program crashed later, inside the allocator.

asan.why: On malloc the left redzone catches the write before libc ever reads the corrupted header. In an arena the 8 bytes are first's slack. The free list (B1.3) keeps its bookkeeping in a side table outside the pool, so there too the 8 bytes are first's slack, which the annotated arm leaves poisoned. Neither pool allocator keeps an in-band header, so glibc's header is the only allocator state this write can corrupt.

hwasan.why: The preceding granule is tagged differently on malloc. HWASan has no public custom-allocator interface, so the annotated columns are UNSUPPORTED, not MISSED (C3.4).

ubsan.why: -fsanitize=bounds needs a statically known array bound; a pointer out of an allocator has none. The row is kept so the report can say UBSan is not a heap tool rather than leaving it out.

lowfat.why: Underflow below a region-aligned base, as case 5.
